questions.prompt: A request callback performs a large synchronous loop. Why do unrelated clients see higher latency?

choices.text: Only the loop request slows because network sockets are independent.
The event loop cannot run other JavaScript callbacks until it yields.
All callbacks get a separate operating-system thread automatically.
The loop is automatically offloaded because the callback handles HTTP.

questions.explanation: One long-running callback monopolizes the JavaScript event loop. Asynchronous socket readiness cannot make other callbacks execute through it.

sources.title: Do Not Block the Event Loop or Worker Pool
sources.claim: Long-running synchronous JavaScript callbacks block the event loop and delay work for other clients.

questions.prompt: A CPU-heavy callback is declared async but contains no yield. What changes about its computation?

choices.text: The runtime preempts its JavaScript loop whenever a socket becomes ready.
The async keyword moves its whole body onto the libuv worker pool.
Every iteration now runs in parallel with all other request callbacks.
It still runs synchronously on that JavaScript thread until it yields.

questions.explanation: async return semantics do not offload arbitrary JavaScript or make its synchronous loops preemptible.

sources.title: Do Not Block the Event Loop or Worker Pool
sources.claim: JavaScript callbacks run on the event loop; partitioning or offloading is needed to prevent expensive synchronous work from blocking it.

questions.prompt: A 100 ms timeout becomes eligible while another callback runs for 200 ms. What does the timer guarantee?

choices.text: It runs after its minimum threshold when the event loop can process it.
It is discarded permanently because its eligibility time was missed.
It runs on a worker thread while the callback continues on the main thread.
It interrupts the running callback exactly when 100 ms elapses.

questions.explanation: A threshold is not a deadline. Busy callbacks can delay a timer beyond the requested interval.

questions.prompt: What does setTimeout(fn, 0) mean for the currently running JavaScript callback?

choices.text: fn is invoked synchronously before the next statement in that callback.
fn starts a dedicated thread that preempts current JavaScript execution.
fn is scheduled for later processing rather than interrupting the callback.
fn is guaranteed to execute before every setImmediate scheduled anywhere.

questions.explanation: Zero does not make a timer synchronous or impose an unconditional global ordering.

questions.prompt: A nextTick callback recursively schedules another nextTick forever. What is the main operational risk?

choices.text: I/O callbacks can be starved before the loop reaches the poll phase.
Only the current client slows because nextTick queues are per socket.
Node guarantees a poll callback between each pair of nextTick callbacks.
The recursion automatically becomes a worker-thread CPU operation.

questions.explanation: The nextTick queue drains before the loop continues. Replenishing it indefinitely prevents I/O progress.

questions.prompt: A script schedules a top-level timeout and immediate. Why avoid asserting one unconditional order?

choices.text: Their names force immediate before timeout in every possible program.
Both callbacks are guaranteed to run before the script finishes.
Their order depends on timing and context, including I/O scheduling.
Both callbacks run simultaneously on separate default JS threads.

questions.explanation: The documented order differs by context. Inside an I/O callback, immediate has specific scheduling advantages; top-level timing differs.

questions.prompt: Which claims explain fairness on a Node event loop? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Declaring a CPU loop async guarantees another thread executes it.
Partitioning computation can create opportunities for other work.
One long callback can delay callbacks belonging to other clients.
Offloading suitable CPU work can keep the main loop responsive.
Every socket owns a dedicated JavaScript execution thread by default.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: async is not CPU offloading. B: Correct: small bounded pieces can yield. C: Correct: callbacks share the loop. D: Correct: explicit offloading moves heavy work away. E: Incorrect: one loop handles many sockets.

A busy callback can delay execution beyond the threshold.
A timeout delay is an exact wall-clock execution deadline.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: elapsed time makes it eligible. B: Incorrect: it is scheduled for later. C: Incorrect: running callbacks are not preempted by timers. D: Correct: loop availability affects execution. E: Incorrect: execution can happen later.
